sentences.text: They went to the river at about eight in the evening.
It was fully dark.
The moon was a specific shape — a bright half moon, sitting low in the eastern sky.
Vovó Nazaré had brought her small dugout canoe, which was bigger than Vovó's own.
It could hold four people comfortably.
They pushed off from the wooden landing.
Vovó Nazaré was at the front with a paddle.
Vovó Marisel was at the back with another paddle.
Tia Gilda and Iracema sat in the middle.
The river was very calm.
The water — because it was the Rio Negro — was so black in the dark that you could not see the surface at all.
Only the moon reflected on it, in a long silver path.
They paddled slowly.
Vovó Marisel and Vovó Nazaré knew where they were going.
It was maybe fifteen minutes downstream to a specific bend where the river widened and where an ancient sandbar came almost to the surface in the middle.
That was the place.
Every year, the same place.
They pulled the canoe up close to the sandbar and stopped there.
They let the canoe drift slowly with the current.
It moved almost imperceptibly.
The night was very quiet.
Even the frogs seemed quieter here.
There were more stars than Iracema had ever seen.
Vovó Marisel began.
She spoke slowly and clearly.
She did not raise her voice — the ceremony was small, and quiet.
She said, "Bartolomea Ferreira, 1802." She paused.
Then, "Maria Ferreira, her daughter, 1834." She paused.
Then, "Ana Damasceno, 1861." Between each name she left a small silence, as if letting the name settle onto the water.
She went through the whole long list, name by name.
Some of the names Iracema had helped her practice.
Some she had not.
Vovó did not stumble.
She said each one clearly.
Iracema counted, without meaning to.
Eighty-three names.
The list took about fifteen minutes.
When she was done she paused for a long moment.
Then she turned to Vovó Nazaré.
Vovó Nazaré said, in her own voice, softer, "Now the recent ones.
From me.
Adelaide, my mother, 2011.
Osvaldo, my husband, 2020.
Camila, my sister, 2023." Silence.
Then she nodded to Tia Gilda.
Tia Gilda said, "Miguel, my brother, 2018.
Silvia, my mother's cousin, 2022." Silence.
Then all three women turned to Iracema.
Iracema was — she found — not nervous.
She had practiced the three names.
She had practiced saying them in a normal voice.
She said, in her own voice, slowly and clearly, "Vitor Damasceno da Silva.
My father.
2018." She paused.
She was surprised that she did not cry.
She said, "Rosa Aparecida Ferreira.
My aunt.
2025." She paused.
Then, in the smallest voice, "Guilherme Ferreira dos Santos.
My classmate.
2024." And then she was silent.
The four of them sat there for a long time.
Maybe five minutes.
Maybe ten.
Nobody spoke.
The canoe drifted very slowly with the current.
The moon moved slightly across the sky.
The stars did what stars do.
Iracema thought about the three people whose names she had just said.
She thought about the eighty-three people from the older list.
She thought about how a river might hold names, if a river could hold anything.
She thought — I do not know if the river heard.
But I feel — I feel — different.
As if something is set down that I did not know I had been carrying.
That is not nothing.
That is something.
When Vovó Marisel felt it was time — Iracema could not tell how she knew — Vovó began to paddle.
They paddled slowly back upstream to the village.
They did not talk on the way back.
When they got to the wooden landing they helped each other out of the canoe.
They walked back up to Vovó's house.
Vovó had bread and tea ready.
They sat at the table and ate a small quiet meal.
Only then did anyone speak.
Vovó Nazaré said, quietly, "Iracema.
You did well.
Your voice was very steady.
You said the names as if you meant them.
That is not always easy the first time." Iracema said, "Thank you." Tia Gilda said, "I remember my first time.
I cried the whole way home.
You did better than I did." Iracema said, "I was not sad.
Just — I was thinking a lot." Tia Gilda said, "Yes.
That is exactly right.
Sometimes when we say the names, we are not sad.
We are — moved.
That is a good thing to feel."
The two other women slept at Vovó's house that night — Vovó Marisel in her hammock, Iracema in the small back bed, and Vovó Nazaré and Tia Gilda on two mattresses on the floor of the main room.
Iracema slept deeply.
She had strange calm dreams.
She woke up early.
She went out to the porch to watch the sun come up over the river.
Vovó Marisel was already out there, drinking her morning coffee.
"Vovó," Iracema said, sitting down beside her.
"Am I going to do it again next year?" Vovó Marisel looked at her.
She said, "That is up to you, sweetheart.
Some women in our family have done it every year of their lives after their first time.
Some have done it only sometimes.
There is no rule." "I want to do it every year," said Iracema.
"For the rest of my life.
If you will teach me all eighty-three names.
So that when you are gone I can carry them.
And then when I am old I can teach them to someone in our family." Vovó Marisel was quiet.
She reached over.
She took Iracema's small hand in her weathered one.
She said, "Then I will teach you.
Every summer.
For as long as I have.
It will take five or six summers to teach you them all.
That is fine.
We have time.
Come.
Let us go make breakfast.
And then this afternoon I will start with the earliest ones.
Bartolomea.
Maria.
Ana.
Come." And they went inside together, and the river went on doing what a river does, which is to hold whatever is put into it, and to keep going.
